title: Trust levels 0-5 from public to steward
notes: Draft §6. Spec has 47 mentions of trust/tier/reputation but those are vote-weighting tiers, not access levels. GENUINELY NEW use of the word ||  LANDED, 2026-10-02, migration 117 + internal/collab/access_policy.go + pkg/sqlite/stashforge_access_policy.go. These sat at `specified` for a whole milestone for ONE reason: the DOMAIN was complete and its 9 tests passed, while the model had no reachability at all -- no migration mentioned an access level and nothing outside internal/collab referenced AccessLevel, LevelFor or Earned. A complete domain model with no caller is not half-built work, it is INVISIBLE work: nothing in a green suite distinguishes 'the access model is wrong' from 'the access model is unreachable', which is exactly how this passed a milestone looking finished. DecideAccess took three inputs and two had nowhere to live -- the operator's ceiling (R062) and the per-user revocable content consent (R026) -- because consent_preferences (migration 102) is about METADATA disclosure and reusing it would be 6a.11's exact conflation. BOTH DEFAULTS GO TO THE SAFE DIRECTION and the contrast with migration 116 is the design: curation defaults to 'propose' because a safe feature must be reachable without configuration, while the ceiling defaults to LevelPublic and consent to off because those defaults would otherwise GRANT SOMEONE SOMETHING. An instance that never touched a setting is not a content-serving instance, and a user who earned Archivist is not automatically a content viewer -- which is the entire point of consent being a separate switch. REVOCATION IS RECORDED, NOT DELETED: 6a.11 requires consent to be revocable and a hard DELETE satisfies that while destroying the question a governance review asks ('when did this user withdraw?'), so revoked_at is set and the row stays, and the migration's CHECK refuses a row claiming granted=1 together with a revoked_at. EarnedFor COUNTS AUDIT ROWS AND CALLS LevelFor, with the thresholds left in the domain because 6a.11 says levels are earned from the audit log and does not fix the numbers; ident solves count DISTINCT targets because five solves of one scene is one contribution. Decide TAKES NO OPERATOR FLAG: 6a.12 says a ceiling is a ceiling and never grants the operator anything the threshold excludes, and the interface has nowhere to pass a bypass. 16 integration tests. Mutation gate 9/9, and THE GATE FOUND THREE REAL GAPS IN MY OWN TESTS: both DEFAULT mutants survived because migration 117 SEEDS instance 1 explicitly so every default assertion was really asserting the seed (fixed by TestTheColumnDefaultsApplyToARowThatDoesNotNameThem, which inserts rows that do NOT name the defaulted columns -- the only path through which a DEFAULT is observable); and the DISTINCT mutant survived because with approvedEdits=0 both counts fall through to the same Curator branch, so the fixture had to satisfy the OTHER half of LevelFor's conjunction for the two spellings to differ. THE GATE ITSELF THEN HAD A THIRD BUG, and it is the one worth remembering: its -run pattern was written out in two places and the copies drifted, so two DEFAULT mutants were reported SURVIVED while the suite it ran could not have contained the test that catches them. Verified by hand that the test kills them ('expected: 0, actual: 5'). A gate's entire output is the word SURVIVED, so a survivor that was never run is the one failure it cannot tell apart from a real finding -- it argues for a weaker gate at the moment a weaker gate is least wanted. Fixed by one SUITE_PATTERN constant plus TestTheMutationGateNamesEveryTest, which EXTRACTS the pattern from the script rather than copying it (a literal in two files is the drift wearing a different hat) and asserts every test in the suite is covered by it. That guard immediately found a fourth real gap: TestTheThreeAccessErrorsAreDistinguishable was not in the pattern. A guard that fires on a correct configuration trains its reader to ignore it -- the same lesson as probe_relay's first run -- so the check is unanchored, mirroring how `go test -run` actually matches. KNOWN GAP, RECORDED NOT PAPERED OVER: EarnedFor passes verificationConsistent=0 and preservationContribs=0 because both are derived quantities (a ratio against a user's own history; a property of what this instance stores) and inventing a formula in SQL would put an access level in the hands of a query nobody reviewed. So LEVEL 5 (STEWARD) CANNOT CURRENTLY BE EARNED, and TestArchivistRequiresBothSignalsNotEither pins the level below it. That is why these are `tested` and not `shipped`.  Levels 0-5 are `collab.AccessLevel` (LevelPublic..LevelSteward, LevelCount=6, MaxAccessLevel); each of the six round-trips through migration 117's CHECK.

title: Public API GraphQL and REST with SDKs and webhooks
notes: TESTED -- commit `3637a5fe3`. 6a.18, "Ecosystem": "Public API over GraphQL (existing 10) plus REST, SDKs and webhooks". The spec names three surfaces and constrains none of their mechanisms, so the design question is what they have in common: each is a way for something OUTSIDE this process to observe the library, and 6a.2's consent is per-instance and REVOCABLE. So the property all three must have is ONE property -- AN OBSERVATION MUST NOT OUTLIVE THE CONSENT THAT PERMITTED IT -- and that is why this is three TRANSLATIONS over one read core (`internal/ecosystem.SDK`) rather than three handlers: three handlers means three places to get the consent rule wrong, and the one that is wrong is the one nobody tests because the other two work. GraphQL was already present from upstream and is unchanged. WEBHOOKS, and the part that CANNOT be solved: a subscriber receives a payload, consent is revoked, and the subscriber holds a copy of an entity it must no longer see -- the bytes left the building and no mechanism can recall them. The usual mitigation is to stop FUTURE deliveries, which does not address the copy already in the other party's log. So the honest position, which is NOT "we solved it": a delivery cannot be un-delivered, and what this side controls is the WINDOW and the PROOF. `Delivery` carries `ShareAtDelivery` -- the share state observed WHEN the payload was produced -- so a receiver can tell per payload whether it was sent under an opt-in that was current then. Deliberately not the consent state: 6a.2's state is revocable and a receiver must not treat "this was published when you got it" as current fact. `RevokeConsent` runs at REVOKE time, not send time, because send time may never come -- if the transport is down a payload queued now sits until it comes back, and a revoke that only affects future sends leaves it there. A "stop future deliveries" implementation passes every other test in the file and fails that one, because nothing is being sent at all. It checks the entity's CURRENT share state, NOT the delivery's proof: a delivery valid when made can be invalid now, and only the current state decides. Dropped payloads are ZEROED, not just filtered out of the returned slice -- a slice that keeps them alive in the backing array is still a store, and the test reads PAST the new length to prove it. Other choices with reasons: an empty event set matches NOTHING (a "default to all" on a broadcast surface turns a misconfigured subscriber into a bulk feed of a library it may not be entitled to); a subscriber's OptOut is SEPARATE from Unsubscribe, because collapsing them makes it possible to implement a revoke as an unsubscribe and leaves "still subscribed, still opted in" reachable; the queue is bounded and drops the OLDEST, because a consumer wants recency and a queue that refused new deliveries would turn a backlog into a permanent outage. NO TRANSPORT: Dispatch returns what it WOULD send, because an outbound HTTP call from a consent-gated surface is where a payload actually leaves and doing it here would couple the consent rule to a network -- so the URL is stored and never fetched by this package, asserted by a method allowlist, since "no transport" has to be a boundary rather than a claim. REST, and the three ways a public surface gets wrong, in order of how badly they hurt: (1) UNBOUNDED READS -- the cap is applied on the way IN from a URL the caller controls and pushed THROUGH to the SDK rather than applied after fetching, because a surface that fetched everything and paginated in memory would be correct and unbounded, which is the failure 6a.16 names; a test asserts the limit and offset REACH the SDK. (2) CONSENT APPLIED AFTER THE READ -- this surface does no querying at all, only translation and delegation, asserted structurally, so there is exactly ONE implementation of the consent rule and it is not this one. (3) ERRORS THAT LEAK -- the SDK's error is NOT forwarded, because a storage-layer error says `entity "scene-1" is opted-out (metadata_share=opted-out)` and every part of that is a disclosure: the name confirms the entity exists, and "opted out" versus "not found" tells the caller which case it is. 6a.21 says an opted-out entity is "neither indexed nor reachable"; an error saying "opted out" makes it reachable as a FACT. So there is ONE answer for every absence, and a test feeds a deliberately leaky error through and asserts none of it survives. Out of range is a CLIENT ERROR, not a silent clamp: a silent clamp looks like the server ignoring the request and the caller cannot tell it should paginate. An origin with a slash, query char or fragment is refused, because 6a.6's origin is a path segment and allowing a slash lets one caller address another's namespace. Entity URLs escape the public id, since an unescaped id containing a slash addresses a different resource -- on a public surface, a way to read something the caller did not ask for. The base URL must be absolute or no canonical URL is canonical. The response echoes the applied limit (a cap is only useful to a client that can observe it) and `Total` is the number RETURNED, because a real total would leak the size of a library the caller may only partly see. 38/38 MUTANTS KILLED ACROSS BOTH FILES, ZERO SURVIVORS, and the seven first-pass survivors were worth more than the fixes: a revoked payload left alive in the queue's BACKING ARRAY (my test asserted absence from Pending(), which a filter-in-place satisfies -- Pending() only reads up to the new length; the same shape as the Holders aliasing in R057, where the write is real and the accessor hides it); Dispatch returned one copy per eligible SUBSCRIBER all carrying the same Delivery.ID, so the caller got N payloads it could not route and the fan-out sort by ID was a NO-OP -- a mutation removing it survived because it did nothing either way, which is a DESIGN BUG rather than a missing test, now fixed by having each copy name its SubscriberID and ordering by subscriber; Subscribe stored the caller's Events slice BY REFERENCE, so a caller reusing its slice could rewrite a registered subscription's event set including widening it; RevokeConsent(nil) PANICKED instead of refusing, and a crash on the consent path is the worst possible failure there -- a crash instead of a revoke. TWO EQUIVALENT MUTANTS are recorded in the test file so nobody re-derives them: swapping the opt-out check after the event match (both branches continue, no side effect, no observable difference), and the sort by Delivery.ID above. STILL NOT WIRED: no HTTP server or GraphQL resolver is mounted and no webhook TRANSPORT is implemented -- deliberately, so the consent rule stays provable without a network. What exists is the translation layer, the delivery validation and revocation, and the shared read boundary that R058's sandbox and R057's pull/rankings/preservation paths already run on

title: Stash app two-way sync push edits pull metadata
notes: TESTED -- all four of 6a.19's capabilities now built. `dfa345cf5` (read direction) and `6253ba226` (rankings + preservation) complete 6a.19, "Two-way sync with the Stash app: pull metadata, push edits through the proposal path, see rankings, contribute to preservation." Previously `specified` because only 2 of 4 existed. PUSH went through the proposal path already; `dfa345cf5` added PULL over a one-method `Peer` transport interface rather than `pkg/stashbox.Client` (bound to stash-box's GENERATED types, coupling the peer protocol to a schema this fork does not control; 6a.19 says a StashForge instance is 'the same client surface pointed at a StashForge instance'). THE DIRECTION OF CONSENT is the trap: a peer returning Published:true claims ITS owner's consent on ITS instance, and 6a.21's rule is per-instance, so the peer's flag is DISCARDED and replaced with the local decision; opted out here -> the row is still returned (discovery needs the metadata) but Published is false. Inverting it would let a peer publish this instance's library by answering a query about it. Only the exact string 'opted-in' publishes. 6a.6's (instance,local) id pair is preserved via Origin + QualifiedID(); the bound is applied locally rather than trusted from the peer; a missing transport is an ERROR, not an empty result, because an empty slice reads as 'this peer has nothing' and gets cached as a successful sync. RANKINGS (6a.16, '#4') -- the enforcement is STRUCTURAL: there is no cached score and no counter anywhere in Leaderboard, because RatingOf folds the vote set on every read. A cached rating falls out of step with the votes it claims to summarise and then the 'truth' is whatever the cache says; the answer to the O(votes) cost at mesh scale is an incrementally maintained value WITH the votes still authoritative, never a counter replacing them. Votes are a SET keyed on voter plus a CANONICALISED pair, so 'a beat b' and 'b beat a' are one matchup -- otherwise one voter plays both sides and inflates both ratings. recordedAt is stamped from the board's own clock and is unexported, because a caller-supplied timestamp is a lever: backdate your votes and decay rewards you. Rating is a Laplace-smoothed weighted win rate (w+1)/(g+2) with an 18-month half-life; the prior is why 1-0 reads 0.667 and not 1.0. A DECAY BUG I WROTE, CAUGHT BY A TEST: recordedAt returned the board's CURRENT time instead of the vote's arrival time, so every vote had age zero and the decay weight was exactly 1.0 -- the decay code ran and did nothing. PRESERVATION (6a.9, 'not a feature') -- the hard constraint is the whole thing: 'For a user who set metadata_share=opted-out, their scene is never a replication subject, and no amount of mesh popularity or a preservation bounty changes that.' So the check is NOT a filter applied to contributions after they arrive: it runs BEFORE anything is registered, and a refused contribution leaves NO policy behind. A later filter would still have accepted the claim, updated a counter and sent a message; 6a.9 is about the subject never being a subject at all. The consent string is compared EXACTLY -- no trimming, no case folding -- so 'OPTED-IN' and 'opted-in ' both widen the surface to nothing rather than to everything, because a peer speaking another vocabulary must not decide somebody else's consent. DefaultReplicas is a FLOOR, not a target: a contribution claiming one replica cannot declare a scene adequately preserved on one instance. Refusal is TOTAL ('refusing is not a partial success') and REMEMBERED -- 'refused' and 'never asked' must not be the same state, or a caller that retried sees a different answer than one that read the policy. BOTH TYPES GRANT NOTHING (6a.16 'grants nothing (6a.10)', 6a.9): GrantsAccess/TrustLevel/Access exist to be false and empty so the prohibition is in the type, and both types are guarded by a method allowlist. THE SURVIVORS WERE THE INTERESTING PART -- 38 mutations, nine survived the first pass. Four were real gaps, four untested properties, one was a mutant of mine that could not differ from the original. Three took three attempts each, all the same underlying trap: WHEN TWO GUARDS CAN BOTH CATCH ONE INPUT, AN OUTCOME-ONLY ASSERTION TESTS THEIR UNION, and deleting either leaves the suite green. (a) 'Empty entity id accepted' survived a test that visibly contained an empty-id case, because that case paired Left:"" with Winner:"alpha" which the WINNER check also refuses; a throwaway probe confirmed Left:"", Right:"alpha", Winner:"alpha" IS accepted with the empty-id guard removed -- a leaderboard row for a nameless entity, reachable by any peer. (b) 'Sort drops the game-count tiebreak' survived twice because I chose entity names where the id tiebreak AGREES with the game-count one; the test only distinguishes them if they point in OPPOSITE directions, so the better-attested entity must be the one whose id sorts LAST. The tie itself had to be SOLVED FOR, not guessed: Laplace smoothing makes (w+1)/(g+2) equal only at specific pairs, and 1-0 and 3-1 are both exactly 2/3. (c) 'Holders slice aliases stored state' survived three times: with the copy removed the returned and stored slices ARE the same array, but assert.Len(stored,1) still passes, because the append writes index 1 of the shared array and only extends the CALLER's len -- the write is real and the store's own length hides it. Holders is also built one element at a time from nil so len==cap always and a plain append can never see the aliasing; the test has to build spare capacity by hand. FIX: assert the message, the array identity, or choose inputs only one guard accepts. 38/38 MUTANTS KILLED, ZERO SURVIVORS. STILL NOT WIRED: no transport is bound to a live peer and no persistence -- the read, push, rankings and preservation paths exist and are proven at the library level, which is what R054 will be built on

title: Developer sandbox with sample data
notes: BUILT (R058) -- commit `793edf042`. 6a.18, "Ecosystem", ends with "a developer sandbox with sample data" and R058 is that line verbatim. The spec gives it one sentence and the plan adds nothing, so the shape came from the requirement's own dependency: R058 depends_on R054 (public API/SDK surface), which is not built, so a sandbox cannot be a live instance with a REST endpoint -- there is no REST surface to point a client at. Built instead is the half that does not depend on the transport: a fixed synthetic corpus satisfying the SDK boundary R054's clients will be written against, plus the guarantees that make the data safe to hand to a third party. THE GUARANTEES ARE THE SUBSTANCE -- a list of fake scenes is a fixture; what a developer needs is to be able to TRUST it, and each guarantee exists because its absence is a concrete way a developer's own library gets corrupted: (1) a sample indistinguishable from real data ships into production -- so Synthetic is a DATA FIELD and the title carries a [SAMPLE] prefix, not a README note, because the README is not what ends up in their database; (2) a sample carrying consent state is mistaken for a real decision (6a.2) -- Share is present and always empty, Published always false, so 6a.21's gate is not satisfiable by sample data at all; (3) an unbounded or unstable set makes every position-dependent test intermittent -- the corpus is a fixed list, bounded by MaxPublicLimit, rebuilt fresh per call so no caller can mutate the shared slice; (4) an un-namespaced sample id collides with a real entity on import -- THIS IS THE ONE THAT BITES: a developer imports sample data into a library that already has a performer with id 42, then imports real data with a different performer with id 42, and without a namespace they are the same row to anything id-based. R060's canonical URLs collide identically, which is why the prefix must also be a single path segment. SyntheticEntity is deliberately NOT PublicEntity -- a sample is not a public entity, and making it one would mean either carrying fields a sample has no business having or leaving a hole where a caller expects them. Origin names the corpus, not an instance, because sample data came from nowhere and pointing 6a.6's (instance,local) pair at a real instance addresses something that does not exist. THE WRITE PATH IS ABSENT BY CONSTRUCTION, reusing R057's positive-allowlist guard -- which then CAUGHT ME: withCount, a method that only changes the corpus size, failed the guard, correctly, since an allowlist cannot tell a harmless method from a write, only from one it does not know about. Rather than weaken the check to "does not look like a write", the entry was added deliberately with its reason, and the test comment says so for the next person. TWO OF MY OWN TESTS WERE THEATRE AND MUTATION TESTING SAID SO: assert.LessOrEqual(len(all), MaxPublicLimit) against a THREE-entity corpus passes whether or not the bound is applied -- a mutation removing q.bounded() SURVIVED and was right to, since 3 is under 100 either way; the bound is only observable on a corpus larger than the cap, or as a request for fewer rows than the corpus holds, and both are now tested, with SampleSet.Count and withCount existing so the REAL Query is exercised past the cap. And the consent test checked SyntheticEntity.Published (what Sample returns) while never checking PublicEntity.Published (what Query returns, i.e. what a client reads) -- a mutation making every Query row published SURVIVED. A consent rule enforced on one representation and not the other is not enforced at all. Neither would have been found by reading the tests: both passed, and both asserted something true about code no client reaches. Paging was the same shape -- nothing passed a non-zero Offset, so a mutation ignoring it survived; pages are now checked to RECONSTRUCT the corpus, since distinct pages could still overlap or skip and a developer paging to the end would silently lose or repeat a row. A THIRD SURVIVOR WAS MY MUTANT, NOT THE TEST: the "unstable corpus" mutant was n--, which is deterministic, so the set is perfectly stable and the stability test is right to pass -- a mutant not modelling the property it is named for proves nothing, and calling that a finding would have been a false positive. The genuinely unstable corpus, using a real toggle, is KILLED. A FOURTH was a CLAIM WITHOUT A TEST: sandbox.go asserted-in-a-comment that titles are distinct past the named three and nothing checked it; a comment stating an invariant is not the invariant. A FIXTURE THAT DOES NOTHING, twice: overriding Sample on a type EMBEDDING Sandbox is silently ineffective because Sandbox.Query calls Sandbox.Sample through the embedded receiver (it kept returning three rows and the test failed for an unrelated reason), and a standalone fixture with its OWN Query goes green while testing the FIXTURE's clamp rather than Sandbox's -- a duplicated implementation of the logic under test is worse than no test, because it is green and worthless. withCount is the third attempt and the one that works. An embedded override the outer type never calls is the same shape as a guard enumerating a set it can see: it looks like coverage and inspects nothing. 21/21 MUTANTS KILLED, ZERO SURVIVORS (sample published, share populated, synthetic flag dropped, title prefix dropped, id namespace dropped, id with a path separator, wrong set name, set not marked synthetic, query unbounded, Query returning published rows, Query dropping the title, Query attributing origin to a real instance, clamp removed, offset ignored, offset always zero, page not starting at the offset, Query no longer satisfying SDK, a write method added, titles not distinct, ids not unique, genuinely unstable corpus). 12 tests green, all 44 pre-existing in the package still green, go build ./... clean. STILL NOT BUILT: the sandbox is sample data only -- there is no live instance, no REST endpoint and no persistence, all of which arrive with R054's transport; and no sample is derived from a real library, which is deliberate (synthetic, never real data) but does mean a developer cannot exercise their own content here

title: SEO public pages for every entity
notes: BUILT (R060 pipeline) -- commit `ffcffdebd`. The consent gate was already built and tested (internal/ecosystem.DecideIndexing); this adds the half that consumes it. `IndexEntity(PublicEntity, collab.ShareChoice, baseURL)` renders the page and describes it to a crawler, and it takes the ShareChoice and calls DecideIndexing ITSELF, so there is no 'render this page' entry point that does not ask -- a render-then-check design would give two paths that both read correctly and only one of which checks. A refused entity renders Page{}, not a 'not found' page: 6a.21 says an opted-out entity is 'neither indexed nor reachable through a public page', and reachable includes returning anything that answers the question. Page{}'s zero value IS the refusal so page.Empty() is a safe guard everywhere, and NotFoundPage() is deliberately a SINGLE function -- two callers rendering two different refusals is how opted-out and never-existed become distinguishable, and a distinguishable refusal IS the metadata consent protects. A test asserts the two render byte-identical. THE ESCAPING WAS WRONG FIRST: I used html.EscapeString believing it escaped for a URL; it escapes for HTML and leaves '/' alone, so 'a/../../b' produced a canonical resolving outside its own entity -- and my doc comment claimed the opposite of what the code did, which is worse than no comment. Replaced with a per-BYTE percent encoder over the RFC 3986 unreserved set only. url.QueryEscape rejected: form-encoding turns a space into '+', which in a path means a literal plus, so 'a b' and 'a+b' would collide. Every escaping defect was found by a mutation, not by reading: '/' traversal, '%' colliding with our own escaping, ':' scheme-injection, '?' query truncation, '#' fragment truncation, '+' the form-encoding trap. 204/204 MUTANTS KILLED, ZERO SURVIVORS, with the character gate EXHAUSTIVE: all 190 non-unreserved byte values individually mutated and every one caught, plus a rule-level test over all 256 byte values so a widened allowlist fails for ANY input rather than only the tabulated ones. 13 tests / 22 subtests green, all 10 pre-existing still green, go build ./... clean. title: Acquire content the user would enjoy automatically with opt-out
notes: Landed 2026-10-03 as internal/acquisition with R076 (one implementation: the queue IS 'what the mesh holds, minus what this instance has, ranked by taste'). 16 tests, mutation 15/15, 60 packages green under unit and integration. §6b.3 defines it in one sentence and the package implements exactly that sentence. NO RANKING IS INVENTED: discovery.Rank is called as it stands, and the ordering test asserts against scores computed by discovery.Score rather than a hard-coded position -- so a second ranker would fail the test instead of quietly drifting the product toward whichever ran last. The difference from a recommendation feed is one filter and one gate, because a feed SHOWS you things and a queue DOWNLOADS them: R083's switch is read HERE and not filtered into the query (§6b.3 requires enforcement at the point the permission is read, not by omitting rows, because #7's note is that a refactor dropping the filter must not silently resume publishing); what this instance holds is subtracted BY LOCAL ID never by title (a title match re-downloads a scene under a slightly different title, which is the duplicate-library problem the mesh exists to avoid); and a refusal is REPORTED as a refusal, never as an empty queue. Two bugs the tests found, both about saying the wrong thing: a not-found error wrapped in ErrSwitchOff (a caller branching on that sentinel would tell an operator 'fetching is switched off' when the switch is ON and the mesh simply lacks the scene -- a different answer wearing the switch's name), and an explicit request for something already HELD reporting as not-found (those need opposite responses: 'nobody has it anywhere' versus 'it is here, here is where'). The mutation run found REDUNDANT GUARDS rather than missing tests, and both were live code that should not have been there: BuildForRequest checked the switch then called Build which checks it again, so deleting EITHER left the suite green -- two guards where one suffices is what lets a future edit drop one unnoticed, so the duplicate is gone and 'a request cannot bypass the switch' is enforced in one place by construction; and the Valid() check was verdict-redundant with MayAcquire, kept only because it produces the ACTIONABLE message ('OFF is not a state this build knows' teaches an operator they have a typo, where 'does not fetch' teaches nothing they did not choose). Wired onto the Manager because a pure function escapes the constructor-wiring test and would have been the sixth fully-implemented, fully-tested, called-by-nothing component; a test pins that the closure reads the switch FRESH per call, since a captured state would still refuse after the operator turned fetching on. Zero weights are used as given rather than replaced with defaults: a caller who forgets them gets a queue ordered by nothing, which is VISIBLE, where substituting defaults produces a plausible order nobody chose.

title: Taste-ranked acquisition queue reusing the mesh recommender
notes: Landed 2026-10-03 in the SAME implementation as R075 -- the queue IS 'what the mesh holds, minus what this instance has, ranked by taste', so the two requirements are one package (internal/acquisition) and one test file. §6b.3's constraint is 'The ranking function is §6a.5's, unmodified. Nothing new is invented here; the mesh's recommender is pointed at a download queue', and that is the part this row actually asserts. NO RANKING IS INVENTED: discovery.Rank (internal/discovery, §6a.5) is called as it stands with the caller's weights, and the ordering test compares against the order discovery.Rank itself produces AND against the per-item scores from discovery.Score -- so a second ranker here, or a rescore, fails the test rather than producing a plausible order nobody chose. The mutation run includes the mutant that invents a local sort instead of calling §6a.5's function, and it is killed. The queue is a VIEW-equivalent: §6b.3 says the taste vector is 'a view, never a counter' (#4), and nothing here is stored -- Req.Weights, Req.Fingerprint, Req.Gravity and Req.Peer are all inputs, so replacing a term takes effect immediately with no recompute, which is discovery's stated 'gravity slider' property extended to the queue. DETERMINISM is asserted rather than assumed: two identical requests produce byte-identical queues, and reversing the input order changes nothing, because §6a.5 ranks an UNORDERED set and a queue that inherited the caller's order would let input order be observable. Ties break on ID by the same rule discovery.Rank uses, so the two cannot drift. A HELD item cannot influence the ordering -- asserted by building the same queue twice with the held item first and last, because a held item that could nudge a score is a filter that has leaked into the ranking. Zero weights are used as given, NOT replaced with discovery.DefaultWeights(): a caller who forgets them gets a queue ordered by nothing, which is visible, where substituting the defaults yields a plausible taste-ordered queue nobody asked for. #6 is enforced structurally: an explicit request bypasses the ranking entirely through discovery.ExplicitRequest and returns with Score deliberately left at zero, so a caller cannot mistake the rank for the reason the entity came back -- 'a term is a magnitude and a constraint is not'.

title: Content plane that does not require peers to exchange routable addresses
notes: Tested via the relay probe (plugins/p2pdownloader/cmd/probe_relay), re-run 2026-10-03: 4 GiB fetched end to end in 2.7s, content hash VERIFIED, and NO ADDRESS CROSSING -- the verifier saw only a host, never a routable peer address. Stated as a PROPERTY not a technology because §6b.4 names the requirement and §6b.7 refuses to name the technology; the probe settles it by RUNNING the candidate. TRANSPORT DECIDED: relay mesh (Option B) over onion routing, on two grounds -- it met R077 where the direct transport did not, and probe 4's cost structure is compatible with R079's alerts. WHAT THE PROBE DID NOT MEASURE, and a production implementation must: relay discovery and bootstrap (the first node has no peer to ask), NAT traversal (a volunteer relay behind NAT is the common case), the relay's own traffic cost and consent model, and TRANSPORT ENCRYPTION -- the probe forwards an opaque payload and proves the ADDRESS property, not that a relay cannot read what it carries. Those four are the remaining step 8.3 work.

title: Manifest plus content hash and a replica counts only when verified
notes: Built as internal/manifest + internal/replicastore (both green), and this row was STALE until now: the code landed on 2026-09-30 and the ledger still said specified, which is the second time in this project a ledger row has outlived its implementation. Non-negotiable #14: a peer saying it stored the bytes is a claim, the same posture the downloader's storage gate takes toward a peer-supplied filename. The manifest is a WHOLE-FILE sha256 with NO chunk list -- a chunk list buys nothing when a replica is all-or-nothing at the scene level, which is what the scanner and file model already assume, and costs wire forever once peers exist. A replica counts toward N ONLY AFTER manifest verification: health is a CHECKED COLUMN and not a counter (no verification_score, no failure_count), verified_at is the evidence for health and is NULL whenever health is anything but 'verified', so the two cannot disagree, and there is deliberately no SetHealth taking a free Health -- only SetSettableHealth, so the compiler rejects the wrong call at the call site rather than a rule in another package catching it. source_endpoint is part of the UNIQUE key per §6a.6: a peer's 'scene 412' is not this instance's 'scene 412', and without it two peers serving one scene collide into a row the mesh believes is a replica it does not have -- a missing copy that health checks pass, which is the worst failure for the mechanism whose purpose is knowing what you still hold. R082's denial gate sits on Record.

title: Preservation alerts when a scene falls below N healthy replicas
notes: Node side landed 2026-10-03 in internal/alert on top of R078's replicastore: high when 0 verified or under half of N, medium when thin, low when short, none at N. A MISSING replica is reported but never raises the band -- §6b.5 makes a failed verification a re-fetch rather than an alert, and preservation.NeedsRepair already owns repair. Candidate has NO traffic field: the way to enforce 'never by mesh-wide traffic' is for the field not to exist. Rank is band + rarity + demand as a fixed-radix number so the band dominates BY CONSTRUCTION -- the first version had an unbounded rarity term and a demand weight that outranked one rarity unit, so a popular low scene could outrank a dying high one, the exact inversion §6b.4 forbids. Demand weight is derived from the demand clamp so the bound cannot drift. DefaultN reads preservation.Default rather than a second literal 3. One unjudgeable candidate FAILS the sweep, because a silently skipped at-risk scene is what this requirement exists to prevent. Mutation 13/14 killed; the survivor scales all band bases equally and is provably order-equivalent.

title: Storage allocation log so an operator can audit what was placed and why
notes: Landed 2026-10-03 as migration 114 + pkg/sqlite/stashforge_allocation_log.go. 33 tests; 59 packages green under unit and integration. Migration 113 records WHICH replica exists, from which peer, and whether it verified -- that is 'what do I hold', and it cannot answer 'why is this instance storing a fourth copy of a scene nobody watches on a disk I pay for', which is the question this requirement exists for. `reason` is NOT NULL and NOT AN ENUM: an enum is a closed list of justifications, and every justification nobody anticipated becomes a NULL, which is exactly the row that needs explaining. What is enforced is that a reason EXISTS and is non-blank. HASH-CHAINED like migration 108's collab_audit and for §5.1's reason -- the owner is not an admin over content and a log any SQL session can UPDATE does not support that; here it bites harder, because the operator most likely to want the log is the one DISSERVED by a rewritten row (a node quietly placing 3x policy would show nothing). `at` is in the hashed payload so an edited timestamp is caught. The log COPIES source_endpoint and scene_id rather than joining mesh_replica: a log that depends on the row it audits can be made to lie by rewriting that row, and ON DELETE CASCADE would take the log entry with it. Probe 3's finding stands -- this answers INBOUND, and migration 110 records the outbound side separately; joining them would let one row claim bytes that never moved. Verified by tampering through raw SQL (edited reason, deleted middle row, rewired link, rewritten timestamp, field migration) with a clean precondition asserted before each. MUTATION 12/14, and the run was wrong twice before it was right: a -run filter silently skipped two tests so three survivors were an artefact, and M11/M12/M13 survived because the schema CHECK catches what the Go guard catches, so the tests passed for the WRONG reason. Both defences are kept -- the Go guard refuses before any SQL runs, the CHECK is the one place a peer cannot talk you out of -- and each is now tested where it is the only thing acting. The two real survivors are provably equivalent (allocationGenesis IS make([]byte,32); Intact=len(Reason)==0 is true on fall-through because Reason is set on the next line), recorded with tests that catch a future edit making either real. Also fixed: errors.Is not == for sql.ErrNoRows (dbWrapper wraps with %w, so an empty log surfaced as a hard error); appSchemaVersion bumped 113->114 in the same commit; and three tests that failed only in a FULL-SUITE run because DbgAuditSelectOne reads one column.

title: Denied and consented-out objects are never replication subjects
notes: Landed 2026-10-03 as internal/subjects, the gate for the THIRD publish path. The exporter and the acquisition queue already refused (internal/api's write-path guard, policy/seeding.go); replication had only half a gate, because preservation.IsReplicationSubject reads MetadataShare -- the §6.2 opt-out -- while the denied TIER is a different rule. Order is load-bearing: denied is checked BEFORE the share choice, since a single 'optedIn && !denied' permits the one subject that matters, denied locators AND opted-in sharing, which is what a preservation bounty would select. §6b.4's 'a bounty never overrides' is enforced by ABSENCE: no force flag, asserted on the package's shape, because a gate with an override parameter invites the one call site that uses it and the reason is always 'this is about to be lost'. MayAccept is a separate function from MayPublish because §6b.5's receiving question is a different question (may this instance hold, not may it send) and one function with a flag cannot express an instance that publishes but refuses to hold. TWO REAL BUGS FOUND BY TESTS: (1) a whitespace-padded tier PERMITTED a denied object -- collab.IsStorageRefused is a raw map lookup that misses on 'denied ' while collab.ParseLocatorTier trims first and reports it known, so table-then-known-check read the space as 'permissive'; fixed by canonicalising once and using the canonical value for both. (2) Decision.Error matched SUBSTRINGS, so an unknown tier classified as an opt-out and an opt-out whose reason matched neither phrase fell through to ErrDenied -- claiming a TERMINAL denial that no setting lifts, the worst direction. Now keyed on a prefix constant every reason starts with; four sentinels not three. Verified: 19 tests, mutation 10/10, and the package is structurally unable to write (AST scan for mutating calls plus a storage/network import ban). 59 packages green under unit and integration.

title: Three-state sharing switch off / fetch_only / full
notes: Landed 2026-10-03 as migration 115 + internal/collab/acquire.go + pkg/sqlite/stashforge_auto_acquire.go, wired into internal/manager. 14 tests, mutation 14/14, 59 packages green under unit and integration. §6b.3's table is TRANSCRIBED into the tests rather than derived from the type: off fetches no / seeds no / uploads no; fetch_only fetches yes / seeds NO / uploads no; full fetches yes / seeds yes / uploads per the existing upload control. THE DEFAULT IS fetch_only and that is the load-bearing decision: an instance that fetches but never seeds leaks no data outward and cannot be made into a source for someone else, so opting a new install in to the harmless half is not a leak, and #7 is about the publish path, which fetch_only does not have. Defaulting to off instead makes preservation unreachable for everyone who never found a setting -- how a feature that exists to prevent loss becomes absent rather than declined. NO PAIR OF BOOLS ESCAPES IT: the obvious repair is a second bool for seeding, and two bools admit fetch=false/seed=true, an instance seeding content it never fetched, which the type cannot distinguish from a deliberate open seeder. There is deliberately no Allowed() summarising the three columns -- a lossy summary of a decision nobody made is a switch somebody reads instead of asking the real question. THE STORE EXPOSES NO FILTERABLE QUERY and that absence is the design: §6b.3 requires enforcement at the point the permission is read and NOT by omitting rows from a query, because #7's note is that a refactor dropping the filter must not silently resume publishing; asserted on the METHOD SET, since a behavioural test passes today and misses a query added tomorrow. A decision my own test forced: plan step 8.1 requires the zero value to be off, a string constant cannot do that, and my first test asserted '' was invalid and failed against my own implementation. The rules are only apparently contradictory -- '' is a Go struct's zero value (nobody chose, so acquire nothing) while 'OFF' is a value somebody wrote (refused, because a peer on a newer core must not acquire), and they stay distinguishable because `off` has a spelling and '' does not. A MISSING ROW reads off while the COLUMN default is fetch_only, because a missing row is a broken database rather than a new install. ParseAutoAcquire returns its OWN sentinel, not ErrShareChoiceInvalid: the switches have opposite remedies, a share refusal wants the user asked again and an acquire refusal wants the value rejected. The store is WIRED and that was not optional -- TestStashForgeStoreConstructorsAreActuallyWired failed on a store that was fully implemented and fully tested and constructed by nothing, now the FIFTH such case in this project, so it is built in internal/manager/init.go with a Manager field. As with R080 one mutant survived because migration 115's CHECK refuses what the Go guard refuses, so the test passed for the WRONG reason; both defences are kept and the Go guard is pinned by its MESSAGE, since a CHECK failure names neither the value nor the valid states.

title: P2P downloader ships as part of core with the module boundary and guards retained
notes: Landed 2026-10-03 as internal/api/stashforge_p2p_guards_test.go -- 5 tests, mutation 7/7, and the downloader module's own 11 packages still green. THIS REQUIREMENT RETRACTS non-negotiable #11, and the implementation is the guarantee rather than a new feature: the module boundary already existed (plugins/p2pdownloader/go.mod, own module, core does not require or replace it) and all five named guards already existed and were tested in the plugin module. What §6b.8 changes is WHERE the guarantee is checked: 'Core code cannot be removed by deleting a directory, so a guard in core is permanent, and a permanent guard is one that has to be right.' Every guard in §6b.8's list lives in the plugin module today, and every guard there is one someone can delete by deleting a directory -- exactly the option the retraction removed. So the guarantee that they EXIST now lives in the core, where a missing guard is a test failure rather than a fact about a directory. Each of the five (consent gate, storage gate, path sanitiser, upload control, ErrRefusedUpFront/ErrRefused) is asserted INDEPENDENTLY, because one test asserting all five passes as soon as four exist. Asserting presence is not asserting correctness -- the plugin's own tests do that -- so this adds the layer the retraction removed and nothing else. THE MUTATION GATE FOUND THREE REAL GAPS IN MY OWN TEST: the first version checked one aliasing regex, and three mutations destroyed the sentinel distinction while keeping both names present AND the plugin compiling -- ErrRefusedUpFront=storage.ErrRefused (missed), ErrRefusedUpFront=errors.New (wrapping dropped), ErrRefused=ErrRefusedUpFront (checked). All three keep the file, the names and the build, and all three destroy the one property the distinction exists for: errors.Is(err, ErrRefused) vs errors.Is(err, ErrRefusedUpFront) is how a caller tells a refusal that left nothing on disk from one that left partial bytes to clean up. The test now asserts every aliasing spelling PLUS the wrapping property itself, because if ErrRefusedUpFront stops wrapping storage.ErrRefused then every caller's existing errors.Is(err, storage.ErrRefused) check stops matching for that case -- and it stops matching SILENTLY, from an edit in another module, which is the risk §6b.8's retraction creates. The four guard-declaration deletions were killed on the first run. The spec's stated cost is PINNED rather than argued: a user can no longer remove the feature, so a future change cannot quietly restore the plugin's removability and claim to have kept §6b.8's guarantees.

title: Cross-repo alignment contract between stash and stash-box
notes: docs/ALIGNMENT.md is the tie-break when the two specs disagree, and changing it amends both specs in the same commit. It owns the shared vocabulary so one word cannot mean two things || LANDED, 2026-10-02, commit PENDING. THE DOCUMENT WAS THE GAP, not the contract. ALIGNMENT.md §9 said check 4 'does not exist yet' and backed it with a measurement: the commons has 'exactly one' path-shaped column. BOTH halves were stale, and the measurement is the part that mattered, because a guard written from it would have been wrong. Re-measured by script over all 94 migrations: SIX address-shaped columns, not one. Three did not exist on 2026-09-30 -- site_urls.url (21), webhook_endpoints.target_url (84), federation_peers.base_url (89) -- so the old list would have blessed images.url and refused the other five, and images.url is the ONLY one of the six that is rendered to a client, i.e. the only one where a file:// is an active primitive aimed at whoever views the image rather than a typo in a human's data. THE ACTUAL WORK WAS SMALLER THAN THE DOCUMENT SAID, and finding that out was the point. I drafted a new schema-scanning guard, then found that R074 had already built it: federation.ValidateImageURL (shape rule -- http/https only, no local-file marker, deliberately NO dns resolution because this box never dials an image url, so refusing a name that does not resolve from here would reject legitimate rows and would be the guard being wrong in the direction that LOOKS safe) and federation.ValidateBaseURL (the opposite -- a peer IS a host this box dials, so it resolves and refuses loopback, private and link-local ranges). I DELETED MY DRAFT rather than shipping a second validator: two predicates for one rule is exactly the drift this document exists to prevent, and I would have been the author of it. All three guards are WIRED, not merely defined, and I verified each call site instead of assuming it: ValidateImageURL from internal/service/image/service.go, ValidateBaseURL from service.go on BOTH create and update peer, and dialGuard from client.go on every dial. The third is the one that matters most and the one a grep for the obvious name misses: the write-time check cannot cover the REBINDING WINDOW, because a hostname that resolved publicly when the row was written can resolve to 127.0.0.1 by the time we dial -- a DNS TTL has nothing to do with when an operator registered the peer, so an attacker with a short TTL walks past a guard that only ran at insert. My first draft of the corrected section claimed ValidateBaseURL was called from resolver_federation.go; it is not, it is service.go and dialguard.go, and I corrected the document rather than leaving the claim standing -- a contract whose own citations are unchecked is the failure this file is about. THE POSITIVE CONTROL IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF and the reason the scan is not the test: the schema was clean on 2026-09-30 and is clean now, so a scan passes vacuously and is indistinguishable from a guard that is not looking. Each predicate is tested by planting the attack, including a bare /etc/passwd with NO SCHEME AT ALL -- the case a scheme check lets through, and the reason the guard is not a prefix test -- and each is paired with a test that the ORDINARY value is accepted, because a guard that refuses everything passes the attack cases and is deleted on first real use. That already happened here once: the first ValidateImageURL reused the existing IsSuspiciousValue predicate, which is the F1 question-text predicate and rejects any value containing http://, so it refused every legitimate image on the column. THE MARKER LIST IS SHARED; THE PREDICATE IS NOT. WHAT THIS SECTION DOES NOT CLAIM, because the document's value is that it can be trusted to say what is unfinished: three of the six columns are operator-typed and SCANNED rather than REFUSED, because refusing them would break real data, so a hostile write reaching one of those is reported and not rejected. Closing that is open work, recorded here rather than left for someone to assume it was done.

title: Automatic metadata acquisition filtered by instance taste
notes: The do-the-same-for-metadata half. Mostly built (6.5 federation plus pkg/stashbox); what is missing is the taste filter, not a foundation. Metadata replicates UNCONDITIONALLY with no N, because the commons is already the durable copy || PARTIALLY advanced, 2026-10-03, commit 6b35c6dd7. The gap is real and is NOT a missing vocabulary map entry. I added performer_ids/tag_ids to the scene and image vocabularies; the unit suite went green and pkg/sqlite's TestVocabulary_EveryFieldIsARealColumn caught it and the change is REVERTED. A vocabulary field is a COLUMN NAME that TargetStore.WriteFieldIfChanged interpolates straight into an UPDATE, and those two are JOIN TABLES -- so the change would have validated, been filed, been approved, then died as a SQL error on the first proposal a user touched. That is the identical defect spec 4.1's studio.url was and the identical thing that guard was built to catch, so leaving it would have re-introduced the very bug the test exists for. The gap needs TWO changes, neither of them a map entry: (1) list semantics -- the field names a set while one proposal carries one entity id, and 'insert into a join table' is not an UPDATE (the additive reading is honest, and the reason a removal is deliberately not expressible, but it is still not an UPDATE); and (2) an AddLink method on TargetStore, which is four column read/write methods and is the surface where a vote becomes a write on shared content -- that wants its own review, not a patch smuggled in beside a map. Recorded as an INVERTED tripwire, TestLinkKindsCannotBeProposedYetAndThatIsTheKnownGap, which asserts the gap is still open, names both steps, and fails the day either lands; it carries a control assertion (scene/studio_id must stay proposable) so it cannot pass by the vocabulary being unreachable, the vacuous pass that once made a write-path guard report clean while matching nothing. The full reasoning lives in vocabulary.go where the next person looks. A REAL BUG surfaced meanwhile, unrelated to links: deleting the Atoi error check in ValidateValue's TypeInt branch SURVIVED mutation, and my first reading -- that it was redundant with the n<=0 test since 'abc' parses to 0 -- was wrong. strconv.Atoi SATURATES on overflow and reports the error separately, so '9223372036854775808' becomes MaxInt64: positive, plausible, pointing at a row that does not exist. Positivity refuses a value that is not a valid id; the parse check refuses a valid id written in a form the parse rejects. vocabulary_overflow_test.go now covers every TypeInt field derived from ProposableFields (so a new int field needs no list edit) with a NotZero guard against a vacuous pass, and MaxInt64 is still accepted so the answer cannot become 'reject anything big'. M7 killed. M10 (TypeInt's explicit empty-string check) survived and IS redundant -- Atoi('') yields 0 and positivity catches it -- so it is kept with a comment saying so, rather than deleted on a wrong analogy with the check above it. 60 packages green unit and integration. || ADVANCED, 2026-10-03, commit e1cdde1fe. The vocabulary blocker is GONE; the autotag WIRING is not. Measured first, because it changed the diagnosis: I filed each kind autoproposal declares through a proposer running the REAL validation and 4 of 5 were REFUSED (only scene/studio_id, a real column, was accepted). So the Curator could file one of five kinds, and the gap was a model change rather than a wiring change. THE FIX IS TWO NAMESPACES, not one map entry: internal/collab/link.go is a closed map keyed on (target, kind) -> (table, idColumn, linkColumn) and TargetStore.AddLink is the operation. A vocabulary field is a COLUMN NAME interpolated into an UPDATE and a relationship is an INSERT into a join table -- there is no SQL that UPDATEs a set, which is exactly what TestVocabulary_EveryFieldIsARealColumn said when it rejected my first attempt. The same kind string means different tables per target (performers_scenes vs performers_images), so the key is the PAIR. I invented all four table names (scene_performers, image_performers, scene_tags, image_tags -- all plausible, all wrong) and TestEveryLinkTableAndColumnIsReal caught it by reading the real tables off a migrated database; verified it bites by putting the invented names back. ADDITIVE ONLY is the safety argument: the field names a set and the value names one member to add, so a removal is not expressible anywhere in the signature, there is no RemoveLink, and the mutant that adds one is killed. A NIL VALUE is refused for a link and accepted for a column, and the asymmetry is asserted so the two rules cannot be merged later by someone who finds them inconsistent. IDEMPOTENCY comes from a different mechanism than a column's: the join table's uniqueness constraint via INSERT OR IGNORE, loser reports added=false -> ApplyAlreadyCorrect with no second audit row; deliberately NOT a read-then-write, which would have the exact race the column path's compare-and-set exists to avoid. A PRE-EXISTING test caught a schema oracle in my own code: TestProposal_VocabularyIsCheckedBeforeStickyRejection requires a non-proposable field to be refused with ErrFieldNotProposable, and my ValidateLink put the field name in the message, making a link refusal distinguishable from a column refusal -- so ErrLinkNotProposable IS ErrFieldNotProposable, one question with one answer, and IsLinkField is the positive question. The gap test is INVERTED to TestEveryKindAutotagCanFileIsNowAcceptedByTheSystem and runs the real validation rather than a stub, because the stub version of that test passed while four of five kinds were refused. Mutation 13/13. STILL OPEN: the 18 autotag call sites write directly, so governance is available rather than in force; the allow-list and its tripwire are unchanged, and the tripwire's comment now records that one of its two blockers is gone. || LANDED, 2026-10-03, commit PENDING. THE 18 CALL SITES NOW GO THROUGH A SINK and the allow-list and its tripwire are GONE -- governance is in force, not merely available. The sink is one interface with TWO methods, and the split is the design finding of this step: a STUDIO IS A COLUMN and a performer or tag is a JOIN-TABLE ROW, so a single AddMatch could not express both. The first version routed a studio through AddMatch as the kind "studio_id" -- a string literal standing in for a concept the signature did not have -- and THE TESTS CAUGHT IT: 18 of them failed on an unmet UpdatePartial, because a recording sink that faithfully implements AddMatch cannot perform a column write. The failure was the design note. So Sink has AddMatch (a relationship) and SetStudio (a field), a studio claim is a SINGLE-WRITER COMPETING claim on one field rather than a second member of a set, and the test that once asserted galleries carry no links is now INVERTED rather than deleted -- its purpose was never 'galleries must be absent', it was 'a target is present only if its join table has been checked'. DirectSink DELEGATES to the same collab.TargetStore the applier uses, so apply and propose differ in GOVERNANCE and not in MECHANICS, and a direct write cannot drift into doing something the approved path would not. The curation mode is a THREE-STATE type (off/propose/apply) with a NEW INSTANCE DEFAULTS TO propose, which is the load-bearing product decision: a library that asserted 4,000 machine-made claims about people on first run is not recoverable by a later setting. A MISSING ROW reads propose, not off, because a missing row is a database anomaly rather than a choice and 'off' would be a scan that silently stopped. Attribution is the INSTANCE OWNER by IsOwner, not 'the first user' and not 'the only user' -- the first names a person who did not run the scan, the second stops attributing at all the moment a second user exists, and an unattributable claim is the state §4.2 exists to forbid. NO FALLBACK EVER: a filing failure is returned, never applied directly, because a fallback that filled the field while the proposal store was down would look like success. THE END-TO-END TESTS FOUND TWO REAL PRODUCTION GAPS that no existing guard could see, and they are the reason this note is long. (1) studio_id was neither proposable nor writable for IMAGE and GALLERY: the column exists on both with a foreign key (migration 13), and autotag has always matched studios against all three target types, so a governed autotag -- the default -- could not file a studio claim for an image or a gallery at all while the direct path could. (2) the LINK namespace had no gallery entries, so the same was true of performer and tag claims on a gallery. TestVocabulary_EveryFieldIsARealColumn reads the propose side and checks each entry names a real column; it CANNOT notice a column that is real, writable and ABSENT, which is not a broken field but an UNGOVERNED one. Nothing checked the reverse either, so the two guards each covered one direction of the same seam and the bug class is 'one of the two maps grew without the other'. THE CONSEQUENCE IS WORSE THAN A CRASH and worth stating: a vote is recorded as applied, the field is unchanged, the audit row says it changed, and nothing ever reports a discrepancy. So TestTheProposeSideAndTheWriteSideAreTheSameSurface asserts the equality in BOTH directions, and its value is measured by re-applying all three omissions: each is CAUGHT, and the write-side one is caught ONLY by this test. WritableColumnsForTest returns the LIVE map rather than a hand-written list, because a helper built from the test author's belief about the schema would make the comparison circular. Opening image/gallery studio_id to votes is the CONSERVATIVE direction -- a vote is required, so the worst case is a rejected proposal, never an unaudited write -- whereas closing it while the direct path can still write the column would be the unsafe one. The nine end-to-end autotag tests were pointed at a REAL DirectSink over the real store: with a recording sink they were not merely weakened but VACUOUS, reporting 'Did not set performer' for every path, which reads like a matching bug and is not one. Mutation 4/4, and one of the four initially SURVIVED as a flag-order artefact in my own gate rather than a test gap -- M1 passed go test with -tags AFTER a package path, so the integration test never ran. The other two survivors were real: no test watched what the sinks WRITE, only where matches went, so sink_writes_test.go now drives both sinks against a fake TargetStore and a real Curator. Its first fake had the link flag named `linkAlready` and returning its negation, which the test caught by asserting the inverse of the real store -- a fake that disagrees with its interface fails the test that uses it, which is the only reason it did not become a permanent lie.

title: Relay discovery and bootstrap for the mesh transport
notes: Step 8.9: probe_bootstrap measured the three options first, then internal/relaydiscovery. Measured: P(>=1 live)=1-(1-p)^N gives N=7 at p=0.5 but N=459 at p=0.01, so a hardcoded list is only viable because peers LEARN each other -- the list is a hint, not a registry. A DHT does not solve first contact: k=20 known nodes precede any query. Learned peers outrank seeds; failures demote with an exponential age-fading penalty bounded BELOW the seed floor; recovery needs no timer. 13 tests. LIMIT: no seeds shipped yet -- WHO runs the bootstrap nodes is undecided, and joining still contacts something (leaks that you joined, not which library).

title: NAT traversal so a volunteer relay behind NAT can serve
notes: Step 8.9/9: cmd/probe_nat then internal/relaybind. R088 claimed a CONFLICT with R077 (hole punching needs addresses exchanged); MEASURED: not a conflict. Being DIALABLE needs an inbound path that NAT denies; DIALING needs an outbound path that NAT exists to allow. A relay needs only the second, so it serves with two outbound legs and no port forwarded -- NAT is not in the path. R077 survives because addresses reach the RELAY (the dispatcher) and never between the endpoints; relaybind Peers() physically cannot return an address. 11 tests. LIMIT, documented per R088: peer-to-peer without a relay is unsupported (not needed -- every mesh path goes via a relay); peers do learn the relay address (inherent to any rendezvous, never what R077 claimed); a home relay is unreliable for reasons NAT traversal cannot touch.

title: The relay's own traffic cost and the consent model that governs it
notes: Step 8.8: internal/relayconsent. Two consents (durable consent to relay + per-frame Admit), additive budget with zero=UNCAPPED, per-origin attribution, kill switch checked FIRST and stopping within the current frame. 15 tests + 10-mutant gate all killed. Deliberately has NO CALLER yet: a cap that only exists on a code path is a cap bypassable by not taking that path, so this lands before R087 discovery. LIMIT: does not bind yet; nothing routes relay traffic through it.

title: Transport encryption so a relay cannot read the bytes it carries
notes: Step 8.7: E2E X25519+ChaCha20-Poly1305 in plugin internal/relaycrypto. Relay holds no key, so "cannot read" is structural not policy; relay forwarding code unchanged. Counter-derived per-frame nonces, const 64KiB frame, random final padding (size-oracle closed). 12 tests + 6-mutant gate all killed. LIMIT: MITM can substitute its own key; out-of-band pinning still needed.
